title: Lectio divina, 3: pray
hookLine: answer God with what the word stirred up

lines: A LETTER FROM SOMEONE WHO LOVES YOU.
cards: A long, careful letter arrives from someone who loves you. You read it slowly. You read it again.
You think about it all day. And then you never write back. Not a word.

Put like that, it sounds strange. Yet it's easy to treat Scripture that way: read it, maybe think about it, close the book. Guigo's ladder has a third step, the one that turns reading into a conversation.

teach.h: FROM THE WORD TO THE ONE WHO SPOKE.
teach.b: Oratio is Latin for prayer, but also for a speech; English gets oration and oratory from it. It means speaking, out loud or inside, directly to someone. Second, the turn.
Reading and meditation are about the word. Prayer talks to the one who spoke it. Guigo says meditation makes the soul see what it lacks, and hunger for it, and then prayer asks.
If your word was burdened, and you found you're carrying something heavy, today you tell God about it. Plainly. Third, the model.
One picture of it is the boy Samuel in the Temple. God calls his name in the night, three times, and he keeps running to the old priest Eli.
Finally Eli tells him how to answer, and Samuel says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." God speaks first; prayer is the reply. Fourth, what kind of answer.
Not a polished speech. Whatever the word stirred up.
Thanks, if it was comfort. Sorrow, if it showed you something wrong. A request, if it showed you a need.
Even a complaint: plenty of psalms argue with God, and the Church prays them in its daily prayer.

teach.h: SPEAK, LORD, FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.
teach.b: Remember the father in Mark who cried help my unbelief? One sentence, with tears. That counts.
The Catechism describes prayer as a living relationship, God's thirst meeting the human thirst for God. Lectio divina gives that relationship something to talk about.

how: In lectio divina Catholics move from reading and reflecting to speaking to God in their own words about what the passage stirred, and in the Mass the congregation answers each reading with a response.

o: reciting set prayers from memory, one after another
a vow of silence kept during the reading
answering God in your own words about what you read

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth

s: oratio is where English gets oration
oratio means a speech as well as a prayer.
prayer in lectio divina has to be formal and polished
it's whatever the word stirred up: thanks, sorrow, asking, even complaint.
Samuel answered God the first time he was called
he ran to Eli three times before Eli told him how to answer.

games.q: you're the boy Samuel, called in the night for the third time. old Eli tells you what to say if it happens again. what do you say?
o: speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth.
games.why: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." God speaks first; prayer is the reply.

practice: Say the verse once more: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Go back to your word and what it stirred up these two days, and answer with one honest sentence, quietly or inside.
If you pray, say it to God as simply as you'd say it to a friend; if you don't, say it to the words themselves, or to the quiet, and let the sentence sit there.

wordCard.voice: Oratio. Latin for prayer and for speech: the third rung, answering back to God with whatever the word stirred up. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: prayer, speech. the third rung of Guigo's ladder.

carryVoice: Your line: answer back. The reply doesn't need to be polished. That's day two hundred thirty-five.

sources.q: Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth.
